Appendix A Training Setup and Recipe

A.1 Full Hyperparameters

All Raw ++ RL runs use a LoRA policy with rank r=128r=128, α=256\alpha=256, dropout 0.00.0, no bias, and target modules q_proj, k_proj, v_proj, o_proj, gate_proj, up_proj, down_proj (task type CAUSAL_LM). For CorVer, the same LoRA shape is used for every model from 33B to 1414B. Random seed is 4242 throughout.

Constant across models.

Table 5 lists the hyperparameters identical for every Raw ++ RL run in the paper.

Per-model differences.

Table 6 lists the hyperparameters that vary across models. Note that the per-device batch size and gradient-accumulation steps are traded against each other so that the effective prompt-batch per optimizer step is 2424 (and the number of completions per step is 24×G=38424\times G=384) for every model.

GRPO sampling and rollout.

Sampling parameters take TRL GRPOConfig defaults except where noted; full settings in Table 7.

Optimizer.

Per-model optimizer choice is 8-bit AdamW for every run except OLMo-2-13B-Instruct, which uses torch-fused AdamW. Adam momenta and epsilon take HuggingFace TrainingArguments defaults (β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, β2=0.999\beta_{2}=0.999, ε=10−8\varepsilon=10^{-8}, weight decay =0=0).

Reward weights and mode.

The headline CorVer settings used in every Raw ++ RL run are listed in Table 8. The three reward channels are summed with unit weight; no separate QuCo or format multiplier is applied.

Logging, checkpointing, evaluation.

Logging, checkpointing, and in-training evaluation parameters are listed in Table 9. Checkpoints are evaluated post hoc rather than during training.

Baselines: framing.

The cross-method comparison in Table 1 reports FoRAG, RLFH, FSPO, and KnowRL under reduced configurations relative to the CorVer runs. We attempted to run each baseline at the CorVer configuration (G=16G=16, max completion length 10241024, full-rank policy where applicable). The wall-clock cost was prohibitive in our compute budget. The structural reason is the reward-call budget of Eq. 5 multiplied by the per-call cost of each baseline’s reward source. The reduced configurations therefore reflect each baseline at the strongest setting we could afford within the compute budget used for CorVer; the resulting comparison is not a head-to-head at matched compute, as discussed in the configuration-asymmetry paragraph below.

Baselines: common configuration.

All three of FoRAG (Cai et al., 2024), RLFH (Wen et al., 2025), and FSPO (Li and Ng, 2025) train a LoRA policy with rank r=8r=8, α=16\alpha=16, dropout 0.00.0, and the same target modules as the CorVer runs above, in BF16 with eager attention and gradient checkpointing disabled. All three are evaluated closed-book: only the question is fed at inference, with no retrieval and no neural verifier or LLM judge call.

Baselines: reward design.

FSPO uses TRL GRPOTrainer with G=4G=4 rollouts per prompt, max prompt / completion length 512512, KL coefficient β=0.04\beta=0.04, a binary ⟨think⟩​⟨answer⟩\langle\text{think}\rangle\langle\text{answer}\rangle format reward, and HHEM-2.1 sentence-level NLI scoring at threshold 0.50.5 for the per-token advantage sign-flip. RLFH uses TRL PPOTrainer (batch 1616, mini-batch 88, max new tokens 256256) with the truthfulness / informativeness reward maps from the original paper. Verification calls a ∼27\sim 27B-parameter Qwen3-family chat endpoint with 88 parallel workers. FoRAG also uses PPOTrainer (batch 1616, max new tokens 256256). Each generated sentence is decomposed into atomic subclaims and each subclaim is verified against the evidence field, yielding a sentence-level factuality score. We adapt FoRAG to the closed-book setting by stripping retrieval at inference. KnowRL (a re-implementation of Ren et al. (2025)) uses TRL GRPOTrainer with G=16G=16 rollouts per prompt, max prompt / completion length 256/1024256/1024, sampling temperature =1.0=1.0, and βKL=0.001\beta_{\mathrm{KL}}=0.001. Its reward, per the paper’s Eq. 2, is the unit-weighted sum of three components: (a) a regex format reward ±1\pm 1; (b) a three-tier LLM-judge correctness reward in {+2,+1,−1}\{+2,+1,-1\} (correct / not-attempted / incorrect); (c) a fact-support reward rfact∈[0,1]r_{\mathrm{fact}}\in[0,1] equal to the fraction of supported atomic facts from the FActScore atomic-fact pipeline with NLI entailment verification (DeBERTa-v3-base-mnli-fever-anli at threshold 0.30.3, γ=10\gamma=10) against the FActScore-bundled Wikipedia knowledge base. Both the judge and the atomic-fact verifier call gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18 at temperature 00. KnowRL deviates from the common baseline LoRA configuration: it uses a higher-rank LoRA (r=128r=128, α=256\alpha=256) with FlashAttention-2 and gradient checkpointing enabled, matching CorVer’s adapter capacity. We adopt this setting for KnowRL because it is the closest prior-method analogue to CorVer (sentence-level factuality GRPO with a verifier-side reward), and its memory footprint at r=128/G=16r=128/G=16 with gradient checkpointing fits on a single A100 within our compute budget.

Baselines: difficulty bins via capability cascade.

KnowRL’s public recipe (Ren et al., 2025) filters its training pool by a one-shot capability criterion: only questions DeepSeek-R1 answers correctly on its first attempt are retained. The stated motivation is that neural-verifier RL gives noisy gradients when the verifier itself cannot reliably judge a question. We extend this idea uniformly to all four baselines with a 33-level capability cascade in place of a single threshold. A question is easy if Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct already solves it under closed-book string-match grading. It is medium if Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct fails but GPT-oss-120B succeeds. It is hard if both fail and a 397397B-parameter Qwen3-family MoE teacher succeeds. The 77B threshold on the easy bin is deliberate. 77B sits at the lower end of the target capability range we evaluate against in Table 1, so the easy bin matches questions a small target can plausibly learn from RL. The cascade is computed once and is target-agnostic, so all sixteen baseline runs (FoRAG, RLFH, FSPO, KnowRL on four base models each) share the same easy / medium / hard partition. The goal is to keep no baseline from being weakened by training on questions outside its own verifier’s reliable judgment range. CorVer does not use this cascade. Its per-target self-filter (§A.4) restricts every training prompt to ncorrect∈[1,G−1]n_{\mathrm{correct}}\in[1,G-1] on the target base model, which is a target-specific and target-adaptive difficulty signal that supersedes a static cascade. The filter difference between CorVer and the baselines is structural, not a per-method tuning gift. CorVer’s per-target self-filter is target-adaptive: it requires G=16G=16 rollouts on the target raw model per candidate prompt. The baseline cascade is target-agnostic: difficulty is computed once with three external models and reused across all four targets. Both filters are nonetheless upgrades over the baselines’ original recipes, which apply no filter at all (FoRAG, RLFH, FSPO) or a single-threshold variant (KnowRL). The two filters differ in granularity rather than in direction. Each method receives the strongest filter compatible with the rest of its training-cost profile. Under our cascade, the baselines are at least as well-prepared as in their original papers.

Baselines: training data and compute.

All four baselines (FoRAG, RLFH, FSPO, KnowRL) train on the same 10,70010{,}700-prompt 33-phase forward curriculum sampled from the cascade bins. Phase 11 (3,5003{,}500 prompts) mixes 3,0003{,}000 easy with 500500 medium. Phase 22 (4,2004{,}200 prompts) mixes 1,5001{,}500 easy, 2,5002{,}500 medium, and 200200 hard. Phase 33 (3,0003{,}000 prompts) mixes 500500 easy, 2,0002{,}000 medium, and 500500 hard. Cumulatively each baseline trains on 5,0005{,}000 easy, 5,0005{,}000 medium, and 700700 hard prompts. The underlying cascade pools contain 9,6779{,}677 easy, 20,49020{,}490 medium, and 766766 hard prompts; only the 10,70010{,}700-prompt curriculum subset enters baseline training. Each baseline divides its own optimizer-step budget into three equal segments and advances from phase 11 to 22 at the one-third mark and from phase 22 to 33 at the two-thirds mark, so all baselines see the same easy / medium / hard exposure ratio regardless of total step count. The 1212 FoRAG / RLFH / FSPO baseline runs use a single GPU per job; KnowRL runs a fixed 200200 optimizer steps with checkpoints every 100100 steps on a single A100. Three of the FoRAG / RLFH / FSPO runs (FoRAG and RLFH on Qwen3-8B, FSPO on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) OOM’d on a single A100 and were moved to H200. Per-cell GPU assignments are in Table 19. For the eval reported in Table 1 we use the latest available checkpoint per run; KnowRL is evaluated at its step-200200 final checkpoint. The FoRAG, RLFH, and FSPO accuracy numbers are upper-bounded by their reduced LoRA rank (r=8r=8); KnowRL is run at r=128r=128 (parity with its original recipe) so its accuracy is not constrained by this factor. Per-baseline learning rates and KL coefficients (with GPU type) are listed in Table 10.

Baselines: configuration asymmetry and the feasibility gap.

CorVer and the baselines do not run at the same configuration. CorVer uses LoRA r=128/α=256r=128/\alpha=256, G=16G=16 rollouts, and a self-filtered learning-zone pool of 4,3294{,}329 to 5,6085{,}608 prompts per target (Table 11). The four baselines share the same 10,70010{,}700-prompt 33-phase curriculum but differ in LoRA rank and rollout structure: FSPO uses r=8/α=16r=8/\alpha=16 with G=4G=4; RLFH and FoRAG use r=8/α=16r=8/\alpha=16 with PPO batch 1616; KnowRL uses r=128/α=256r=128/\alpha=256 with G=16G=16. Only KnowRL matches CorVer’s LoRA rank. This asymmetry is not arbitrary. CorVer’s reward is millisecond-scale: one 0.50.5B extractor forward plus one mmap Infini-gram lookup per sentence. Each baseline’s neural-verifier or LLM-judge reward is multiple orders of magnitude more expensive per call. Bringing the baselines up to CorVer’s configuration would multiply that per-call cost by the reward-call budget of Eq. (5). Figure 4 and Appendix C.4 show this configuration is structurally prohibitive for the baselines under any compute budget we considered. We therefore do not claim that CorVer is a stronger sentence-level credit-assignment method at fixed compute. We claim instead that CorVer’s reward design admits a deployable configuration the four baselines cannot reach. The accuracy gains in Table 1 are the consequence of this feasibility gap. Matching CorVer down to any baseline configuration would hide this deployable-advantage gap. Matching baselines up to CorVer’s configuration is the infeasibility shown by Figure 4.

A.2 Datasets and Evaluation Protocol

Evaluation datasets.

Every canonical CorVer run evaluates the final checkpoint on five closed-book QA datasets in series: TriviaQA validation (17,94417{,}944 questions), NQ-Open validation (3,6103{,}610), PopQA test (14,26714{,}267), SimpleQA (4,3264{,}326), and TruthfulQA (817817). Each TriviaQA record carries a question, a primary answer, and an alias list.

Training pools.

The candidate question pools are constructed from NQ-Open (train split) and WebQuestions (train and test splits) through a multi-step cleaning pipeline. The pipeline applies deduplication, question refinement via an LLM, and Wikipedia entity grounding that removes questions whose entities cannot be matched to any Wikipedia article. Two pool sizes result from different construction iterations: a 9,6809{,}680-question pool and a 13,56013{,}560-question pool that incorporates additional data from the same sources. The 13,56013{,}560-pool is a same-source same-pipeline sample-size extension of the 9,6809{,}680-pool: it adds more questions drawn from NQ-Open and WebQuestions under the identical dedup, LLM-refine, and Wikipedia entity-grounding pipeline, with no new datasets or new cleaning rules. Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct use the 9,6809{,}680-question pool; Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, and OLMo-2-13B-Instruct use the 13,56013{,}560-question pool. All pools are then filtered per-model by the learning-zone self-filter of §4.

Self-filter procedure.

For each candidate question we sample G=16G=16 completions from the target raw model (no LoRA) at temperature 0.70.7, top-p=0.95p=0.95, max new tokens =512=512. Each completion is graded by the same string-match grader used at evaluation, giving an integer ncorrect∈[0,16]n_{\mathrm{correct}}\in[0,16] per question. The default keep range is 1≤ncorrect≤G−1=151\leq n_{\mathrm{correct}}\leq G-1=15. Questions the raw model always answers correctly (ncorrect=16n_{\mathrm{correct}}=16) and questions the raw model never answers correctly (ncorrect=0n_{\mathrm{correct}}=0) are therefore dropped. Two of the smaller-model configurations additionally mix in a fixed number of ncorrect=16n_{\mathrm{correct}}=16 “anchor” questions: 1,0001{,}000 for Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and 800800 for Qwen3-4B.

String-match grading.

The training judge and the evaluation grader share the same normalization routine: NFKD normalize, lowercase strip, replace stand-alone articles (a, an, the) with spaces, replace non-word punctuation with spaces, and collapse whitespace. A predicted answer matches a gold answer (or alias) if their normalized forms are equal or one is a substring of the other. Aliases are taken from the alias list at evaluation and from a semicolon-separated answer string at training. The string-match grader emits one of three labels per completion. The training judge maps them to scalar rewards as GOOD =+2.0=+2.0, BAD =−1.0=-1.0, and NOT-ATTEMPTED =−1.0=-1.0 (referred to as NA in the main text). Refusals are rewarded the same as wrong answers, so the trainer does not reward abstention.

Format-correct rule and answer extraction.

A completion is considered format-correct if it contains ⟨think⟩…⟨/think⟩…⟨answer⟩\langle\text{think}\rangle\ldots\langle/\text{think}\rangle\ldots\langle\text{answer}\rangle; the closing ⟨/answer⟩\langle/\text{answer}\rangle tag is intentionally not required, so truncated outputs are not unfairly penalized. Answer extraction takes the substring after the first ⟨answer⟩\langle\text{answer}\rangle tag, up to the matching ⟨/answer⟩\langle/\text{answer}\rangle if present and to the end of the completion otherwise, then strips surrounding whitespace.

Format anti-hack constraints.

In addition to the tag-presence check, the format reward enforces three constraints on the ⟨think⟩\langle\text{think}\rangle content: (i) at least 30 characters, (ii) at least one alphabetic character, and (iii) the first non-whitespace character must not be “<<”. These rules were added after observing reward hacking on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, where the policy learned to emit an effectively empty ⟨think⟩\langle\text{think}\rangle block (e.g. an immediate ⟨/think⟩\langle/\text{think}\rangle followed by reasoning outside the tags) to collect the format reward without performing genuine reasoning. Bin Tarek and Beheshti (2025) document the same failure mode in medical QA and propose composite penalties as a mitigation; our constraints address the same exploit with simpler regex rules. The constraints are applied uniformly across all models reported in this paper.

NA (refusal) detection.

A prediction is treated as a refusal if its lower-stripped form is empty, “i don’t know”, or “i do not know”. The QuCo scorer uses a slightly broader substring pattern internally; the eval and training judges use the strict-equality rule above.

A.3 Generation Prompt

Training-time rollout prompt (CorVer).

The shared system prompt used by every canonical CorVer training run (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B, OLMo-2-13B-Instruct, Qwen3-14B) is the following “light prompt ++ anti-loop” string. The user message is the raw question, and the chat is constructed by each model’s native chat template (no custom override).

⬇
Answer using this exact format:
<think>brief reasoning</think>
<answer>direct answer</answer>
Rules:
- Keep the entire response under 1000 tokens.
- In <think> AND <answer>, always use full entity names; never pronouns (he, she, it, they, this, that, them, his, her, its, their). Repeat the entity name each sentence.
- Do not loop or repeat the same point or phrase.
- If you genuinely do not know, reply exactly: <think>unknown</think><answer>I don’t know</answer>

Baseline training prompts.

The four baselines (FoRAG, RLFH, FSPO, KnowRL) train under each method’s own published system prompt; we do not substitute the CorVer training prompt above. Every baseline prompt requires a ⟨think⟩\langle\text{think}\rangle / ⟨answer⟩\langle\text{answer}\rangle format (or an equivalent reasoning / answer separator) so the same string-match grader can extract a final answer, but the body text differs across methods. At evaluation time all checkpoints use the unified evaluation prompt described next, which is short and method-agnostic, so the eval-side comparison is not affected by training-prompt differences.

Evaluation prompt.

At evaluation the system prompt is lighter, containing only the format rule and the IDK clause:

⬇
Answer using this exact format:
<think>brief reasoning</think>
<answer>direct answer</answer>
If you genuinely do not know, reply exactly: <think>unknown</think><answer>I don’t know</answer>

For trained checkpoints (when a LoRA adapter is loaded), the eval prompt additionally appends the line “Do not loop or repeat the same point or phrase.” This anti-loop line is already part of the training-time rollout prompt shown above. Appending it at evaluation aligns the trained-checkpoint eval distribution with its training distribution. It also mitigates the post-RL repetition mode-collapse that trained policies exhibit on long-form completions. The raw instruction-tuned models do not exhibit this repetition behavior. We observed that appending the same anti-loop line to the Raw eval prompt produced a small accuracy decrease, presumably because the extra rule adds prompt complexity that the un-trained policy is not robust to. The raw baseline is therefore evaluated under the lighter prompt, which gives it its strongest configuration. The Raw vs CorVer gaps in Table 1 and Figure 3 are therefore, if anything, conservative lower bounds. Within each group the prompt is applied uniformly. Every raw baseline uses the lighter prompt, and every LoRA-loaded checkpoint (KnowRL, FoRAG, RLFH, FSPO, and CorVer) uses the anti-loop prompt. Cross-method comparisons among trained checkpoints are therefore not affected by this asymmetry.

Evaluation sampling.

vLLM sampling parameters for evaluation: temperature =0.0=0.0 (greedy decoding), top-pp unused, max new tokens =1000=1000, max model length =1,512=1{,}512 (max new tokens +512+512), frequency penalty unset (default 0.00.0), and stop tokens chosen dynamically from <|im_end|>, <|endoftext|>, <|eot_id|> according to which ones exist in the policy tokenizer’s vocabulary.

A.4 Per-Model Training Set Sizes after Self-Filter

The per-model training pool is filtered with the same rule described in §4. We sample G=16G=16 completions from the raw instruction-tuned model under the CorVer generation prompt and string-match grader, count ncorrect​(x)∈{0,1,…,16}n_{\mathrm{correct}}(x)\in\{0,1,\ldots,16\} correct completions per question, and retain only questions with ncorrect∈[1,N−1]n_{\mathrm{correct}}\in[1,N-1] (the learning zone, with N=16N=16). Table 11 reports the resulting per-model training set sizes. The same self-filtered set is used by every ablation variant in Table 2 except A4, which by construction trains on the unfiltered candidate pool. Accuracy differences among the remaining variants are therefore not confounded with differences in the training set.

Reading the table.

Each row’s three bucket counts sum exactly to its source pool size (9,6809{,}680 or 13,56013{,}560, as listed in the Pool column). Two runs further mix in fixed anchor questions on top of the retained learning-zone count (not shown in the table): 1,0001{,}000 for Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and 800800 for Qwen3-4B. Across the six models, the share of nc=0n_{c}=0 questions ranges from 25.4%25.4\% (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct) to 48.0%48.0\% (Qwen3-4B), and the share of nc=16n_{c}=16 ranges from 18.2%18.2\% (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) to 30.2%30.2\% (Qwen3-14B). The retained learning-zone size ranges from 4,3294{,}329 (Qwen3-4B) to 5,6085{,}608 (OLMo-2-13B-Instruct) and determines the per-step number of distinct prompts available to GRPO at G=16G=16.

Appendix B Co-occurrence Reward Design and Validation

B.1 Co-occurrence Reward Implementation Details

Triplet extractor.

The subject-object-relation triplet extractor is the QuCo-extractor-0.5B model of Min et al. (2025), a Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct fine-tuned on QuCo-RAG synthetic data. We run it with max new tokens 256256 in BF16, with left-padded batches of size 3232. One extractor is loaded per training process (lazy-init, singleton scope). The extractor is prompted to emit one of four outputs: an [entity, relation] pair for question sentences (single relation only for multi-hop questions); a [head, relation, tail] triple for declarative sentences carrying one knowledge triple; the empty list when no factual semantic content is present; or a list of multiple triples otherwise. The output is parsed by a tolerant routine that handles nested brackets, smart quotes, escaped characters, and commas inside multi-token entity strings.

Per-sentence triplet to reward.

For each sentence, the implementation deliberately keeps at most one ternary triplet: the first valid [head, relation, tail] from the extractor whose head and tail are non-empty strings and not pronouns. There is no max / mean / top aggregation across multiple triplets in a sentence. Triplet extraction failure, a non-ternary triplet, or both endpoints being pronouns yields no query and a neutral reward ric=0.0r_{i}^{\mathrm{c}}=0.0 for that sentence. Sentence splitting uses a punctuation-based regex on .!? boundaries. Both ⟨think⟩\langle\text{think}\rangle and ⟨answer⟩\langle\text{answer}\rangle blocks are scored with equal weight after tag stripping.

Word-level co-occurrence query.

Rather than literal entity strings, we build a word-level conjunctive (CNF / AND) query from the head and tail content words. Stop words from a closed-class list of 3535 tokens (articles, common prepositions, auxiliary verbs, basic connectives, and the pronoun “it”; the full list is reproduced in our code release) are stripped. Capitalized non-stop words (proper nouns) are preferred, falling back to all non-stop words longer than 22 characters, deduplicated while preserving order. At least 22 words are required, otherwise the reward is neutral 0.00.0. The remaining words are joined by AND and sent to the Infini-gram CNF count routine.

Penalty mapping.

Given the corpus co-occurrence count cc, the per-sentence reward is

ric={0.0if no valid triplet (count is None)−0.3if ​c=0−0.1if ​0<c<50.0if ​5≤c<20+0.1if ​c≥20.r_{i}^{\mathrm{c}}=\begin{cases}0.0&\text{if no valid triplet (count is None)}\\ -0.3&\text{if }c=0\\ -0.1&\text{if }0<c<5\\ 0.0&\text{if }5\leq c<20\\ +0.1&\text{if }c\geq 20.\end{cases}

This is the four-tier mapping referenced as Eq. (2) in the main text.

Token alignment.

The alignment σ\sigma is built by stripping the ⟨think⟩\langle\text{think}\rangle and ⟨answer⟩\langle\text{answer}\rangle tags, splitting the concatenated text by a punctuation-based regex, and assigning each token to the sentence whose character span contains its tokenizer midpoint. Only tag positions and inter-sentence whitespace receive σ⁡(t)=0\sigma(t)=0. Reasoning sentences in the ⟨think⟩\langle\text{think}\rangle block are therefore scored by the same QuCo reward as answer sentences. If the per-completion alignment rate falls below 0.50.5, the sentence-level QuCo signal is dropped. The completion then falls back to the response-level return Rr​(x,y)=λj​Rj​(x,y)+Rf​(y)R^{\mathrm{r}}(x,y)=\lambda_{\mathrm{j}}R^{\mathrm{j}}(x,y)+R^{\mathrm{f}}(y) for all of its tokens. The training-time alignment rate and fallback rate are logged at every step. In completed runs the alignment rate is consistently ≥0.99\geq 0.99 and the fallback rate is below 1%1\%. The per-token return formula, restating Eq. (4), is

Rt​(x,y)=\displaystyle R_{t}(x,y)\;=\; Rr​(x,y)\displaystyle R^{\mathrm{r}}(x,y)
+[σ(t)>0]⋅λc⋅rσ⁡(t)c.\displaystyle+\mathbf{1}\!\left[\sigma(t)>0\right]\cdot\lambda_{\mathrm{c}}\cdot r_{\sigma(t)}^{\mathrm{c}}.

Infini-gram index.

The corpus is the English Wikipedia dump 20231101.en, containing 6,407,8146{,}407{,}814 articles tokenized to approximately 5.5×1095.5\times 10^{9} tokens by the LLaMA-2 BPE tokenizer (vocab size 32,00032{,}000); a leading-space token (id 2987129871) is stripped from queries. The on-disk index is version 44, with a u16 token dtype, maximum per-clause frequency 500,000500{,}000, and a maximum inter-clause distance of 1,0001{,}000 tokens, served by mmap at training time. Counts are produced as a CNF over content tokens, bounded by the maximum inter-clause distance so that matched positions span at most 1,0001{,}000 tokens between clauses. The resulting cic_{i} therefore measures position-level co-occurrence within a bounded window rather than unbounded document-level co-occurrence.

Window-size choice.

The 1,0001{,}000-token inter-clause window is inherited from Min et al. (2025), who adopt it as the default in their inference-time pipeline because it roughly matches passage-level context and provides a natural semantic boundary for co-occurrence verification. Their sensitivity analysis on 2WikiMultihopQA and HotpotQA varies the window ω∈{50,100,250,500,1,000,2,000}\omega\in\{50,100,250,500,1{,}000,2{,}000\} and reports at most a 1.41.4-point EM swing across the range, indicating the choice is not load-bearing; larger windows yield slightly higher co-occurrence counts and smaller windows trigger more retrievals in their pipeline. We do not rerun this sensitivity sweep for the training-time reward, and treat 1,0001{,}000 as a well-supported default.

Cache and latency.

The headline pipeline uses the local mmap Infini-gram engine with no in-memory cache; every per-sentence query goes through the CNF count routine directly. Per-query latency is millisecond-scale on the single A100 setup. Aggregate end-to-end reward cost is reported in the wall-clock comparison of the main text.

B.2 Zero-Count Penalty Sensitivity

To validate the choice of the zero-count co-occurrence penalty ric​(ci=0)=−0.3r_{i}^{\mathrm{c}}(c_{i}=0)=-0.3 in Eq. (2), we sweep its value over {−0.1,−0.2,−0.3,−0.5,−1.0}\{-0.1,-0.2,-0.3,-0.5,-1.0\} while holding all other reward bins, training hyperparameters, and the base model fixed. Each variant retrains Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct under the canonical CorVer recipe and is evaluated on the full TriviaQA validation set (N=17,944N=17{,}944); Figure 6 reports the resulting change in accuracy relative to the −0.3-0.3 baseline.

Both weaker penalties (−0.1-0.1, −0.2-0.2) and stronger penalties (−0.5-0.5, −1.0-1.0) underperform the canonical −0.3-0.3 setting, with −0.2-0.2 as the worst point at −6.55-6.55 pp. The sweep is therefore consistent with −0.3-0.3 being a sweet spot rather than an arbitrary choice.

B.3 Sentence-Level Aggregation and Relation-Aware Demotion: Mechanism Details

This subsection supplements the empirical comparison in §6.4 (Table 4) with rigorous variant definitions, a worked example, and the mechanism analyses behind the topline numbers reported there.

Variants.

All three variants share the four-tier mapping of Eq. (2), the closed-class stop-word list and content-word CNF query of §B.1, the 1,0001{,}000-token Infini-gram inter-clause window, the per-token alignment σ\sigma, and the CorVer training hyperparameters of §A.1. They differ only in how the per-sentence co-occurrence count cic_{i} is computed before Eq. (2) is applied. First (canonical CorVer) scans the extractor output in order, stops at the first ternary triplet (h,r,t)(h,r,t) whose head and tail are non-empty and non-pronominal, submits a single CNF query over the content words of hh and tt, and passes the resulting count cic_{i} through Eq. (2); the per-sentence cost is one Infini-gram lookup. Min scans every valid ternary triplet (h(j),r(j),t(j))(h^{(j)},r^{(j)},t^{(j)}) in the sentence, submits one CNF query per triplet, and sets ci=minj⁡ci(j)c_{i}=\min_{j}c_{i}^{(j)} before applying Eq. (2); the per-sentence cost is JJ lookups, where JJ is the number of valid triplets emitted by the extractor. RelCheck (following the inference-time pipeline of Min et al. (2025), Appendix A.10) computes the head-plus-tail count cic_{i} as in First; if ci<20c_{i}<20 the sentence reward is ricr_{i}^{\mathrm{c}} from Eq. (2) directly; otherwise a second CNF query is submitted with the content words of the relation rr added to the AND conjunction, and if this relation-augmented count is zero the sentence reward is demoted from +0.1+0.1 to −0.05-0.05 (otherwise +0.1+0.1 is retained). The per-sentence cost of RelCheck is one lookup when ci<20c_{i}<20 and two lookups otherwise.

Worked example.

Consider the completion “Mario Camerini directed Il Seduttore. The film starred Sophia Loren.”, where the first sentence triggers two extracted triplets: (1) (Mario Camerini,directed,Il Seduttore)(\text{Mario Camerini},\text{directed},\text{Il Seduttore}) with c(1)=50c^{(1)}=50, and (2) (Il Seduttore,starred,Sophia Loren)(\text{Il Seduttore},\text{starred},\text{Sophia Loren}) with c(2)=0c^{(2)}=0 (a fabricated cast member). First returns ci=50c_{i}=50 and assigns ric=+0.1r_{i}^{\mathrm{c}}=+0.1, missing the second triplet. Min returns ci=min⁡(50,0)=0c_{i}=\min(50,0)=0 and assigns ric=−0.3r_{i}^{\mathrm{c}}=-0.3, correctly flagging the fabricated cast member but at the cost of treating the entire sentence as unsupported. RelCheck returns ci=50c_{i}=50 as in First; the relation-augmented query over (Mario Camerini, directed, Il Seduttore) is non-zero, so ric=+0.1r_{i}^{\mathrm{c}}=+0.1 is retained. If the model instead generated “Sophia Loren directed Il Seduttore”, the head-plus-tail count over (Sophia Loren, Il Seduttore) may still be positive from incidental co-occurrence elsewhere in Wikipedia, while the relation-augmented count is zero, and RelCheck demotes the reward from +0.1+0.1 to −0.05-0.05.

Why Min underperforms.

On any sentence with two or more extracted triplets, the probability that at least one query returns a zero count is high, both because secondary triplets are often extracted with weaker entity spans and because Min commits the entire sentence to its worst-case count. The resulting reward gradient pushes the policy toward shorter completions: training logs show the mean completion length collapsing from approximately 150150 tokens under First to between 3535 and 4646 tokens under Min, and the refusal rate falling from 5.04%5.04\% to 0.33%0.33\%. Shorter completions reduce the per-sentence chance of triggering a −0.3-0.3 penalty, but also reduce the chance of stating the correct gold answer, which accounts for the −4.97-4.97 pp accuracy drop. Min therefore fails not because it identifies fewer factual errors than First, but because the aggregation rule couples factuality and length in a way that the policy can exploit.

Why RelCheck underperforms.

Min et al. (2025) present relation-aware verification as an optional extension, not the canonical setting, and Appendix A.10 of their paper gives the reason. The entity-only check is intentionally asymmetric. A zero entity count c⁡(h,t)=0\mathrm{c}(h,t)=0 strongly signals hallucination risk, but c⁡(h,t)>0\mathrm{c}(h,t)>0 does not certify the relation: the entities may co-occur under different relations or in unrelated contexts. Adding the relation to the CNF query also introduces surface-form noise. Relational predicates exhibit high lexical variability, while named entities are lexically stable. The same relation “directed” appears in Wikipedia as “directing”, “was the director of”, and many other variants. A literal-token relation lookup may therefore return zero on a correct claim that simply uses a different surface form. Empirically, the demotion from +0.1+0.1 to −0.05-0.05 reduces accuracy by 0.870.87 pp and raises the refusal rate from 5.04%5.04\% to 6.58%6.58\%. The relation-augmented lookup also doubles the per-sentence Infini-gram cost on the high-frequency bucket, raising end-to-end training wall clock by approximately 70%70\%. Min et al. (2025) report a parallel cost trade-off in their inference-time pipeline: +39+39 to +51%+51\% retrieval frequency for +2.1+2.1 to +2.4+2.4 EM. In our training-time GRPO setting, the combined accuracy and cost trade-off favors retaining the entity-only First variant.

B.4 CorVer Algorithm

Algorithm 1 summarizes the per-step CorVer procedure described in §3.4 and §4. Each step samples GG completions from a learning-zone prompt, extracts a subject-object pair and computes ricr_{i}^{\mathrm{c}} for every sentence in the completion (sentences from both the ⟨think⟩\langle\text{think}\rangle and ⟨answer⟩\langle\text{answer}\rangle blocks are parsed jointly, as in §3.1), builds the token-to-sentence alignment σ\sigma with the per-completion fallback, and assembles the per-token raw returns of Eq. (4) before the GRPO group-normalization and clipped-surrogate update.

B.5 Human Audit of the Four-Tier Co-occurrence Reward

We manually audited 700700 sentences sampled from training-time generations of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on TriviaQA prompts (drawn from both the ⟨think⟩\langle\text{think}\rangle and ⟨answer⟩\langle\text{answer}\rangle blocks in proportion to how they appear in the reward stream). The audit covers all five precision regimes of the four-tier mapping. It is the empirical basis for two distinct claims about Eq. (2): that the co-occurrence count cic_{i} is a directional proxy for sentence-level factuality (§6.1), and that the bucket boundaries at ci=0c_{i}=0, 55, and 2020 are placed where the empirical precision actually transitions.

Sample construction.

The audit was built in two passes. The first pass targeted the two extreme buckets. We sampled 200200 sentences from the high-frequency bucket (ci≥20c_{i}\geq 20, mapped to ric=+0.1r_{i}^{\mathrm{c}}=+0.1) and 200200 from the zero-frequency bucket (ci=0c_{i}=0, mapped to ric=−0.3r_{i}^{\mathrm{c}}=-0.3). The second pass extended coverage to the intermediate range. We sampled 100100 sentences in each of 1≤ci≤41\leq c_{i}\leq 4, 5≤ci≤95\leq c_{i}\leq 9, and 10≤ci≤1910\leq c_{i}\leq 19. The split at ci=10c_{i}=10 is deliberately placed inside the middle reward bucket 5≤ci<205\leq c_{i}<20, so the audit can probe a candidate boundary that Eq. (2) does not use. The total is 200+100+100+100+200=700200+100+100+100+200=700 sentences. For each sentence we record the full text, the extracted subject-object pair, and the resulting Infini-gram AND query.

Annotation protocol.

Five paper co-authors independently annotated every sentence in the two extreme buckets. Each annotator verified the claim with web search before labelling its factual correctness as correct or incorrect. The final label for each of those 400400 sentences is the majority vote across the five annotators. The 300300 intermediate-bucket sentences were labelled by the paper authors under the same web-search rubric. The verdict for every sentence is independent of whether the surrounding QA completion produces the gold answer. We are auditing the reward signal, not the eval grader.

Two-bucket precision at the extremes.

Table 12 reports the per-bucket precision on the 400400-sentence pilot. High-frequency sentences are factually correct 81.0%81.0\% of the time. Zero-frequency sentences are factually incorrect 76.0%76.0\% of the time. Both buckets exceed 76%76\% precision in the direction matched to the sign of ricr_{i}^{\mathrm{c}}. The bidirectional correlation supports the use of subject-object co-occurrence frequency as a directional proxy for sentence-level factuality at the two extremes of Eq. (2). It does not establish equivalence with a predicate-aware verifier.

Five-bucket calibration curve.

Figure 5 in §6.1 and Table 13 report P⁡(correct∣ci)P(\mathrm{correct}\mid c_{i}) in each of the five buckets with Wilson 95%95\% confidence intervals. Precision rises monotonically with cic_{i}, from 24.0%24.0\% at ci=0c_{i}=0 to 81.0%81.0\% at ci≥20c_{i}\geq 20. The two boundaries used by Eq. (2) sit at clearly visible precision transitions. The ci=5c_{i}=5 boundary corresponds to a +17.0+17.0 pp jump (from 53.0%53.0\% to 70.0%70.0\%). The ci=20c_{i}=20 boundary corresponds to a +8.0+8.0 pp jump (from 73.0%73.0\% to 81.0%81.0\%). The largest single jump is the +29.0+29.0 pp transition across ci=0c_{i}=0, consistent with the strongest penalty −0.3-0.3 being assigned to the zero-count bucket. The un-used boundary ci=10c_{i}=10 corresponds to only a +3.0+3.0 pp transition (from 70.0%70.0\% to 73.0%73.0\%). This supports the choice not to subdivide the 5≤ci<205\leq c_{i}<20 reward bucket.

Interpretation and residuals.

The residual 24%24\% of zero-frequency sentences that are in fact correct represent rare-but-correct facts whose reward is under-credited under the current bucketing. The residual 19%19\% of high-frequency sentences that are incorrect represent well-supported entity co-occurrences attached to a wrong predicate. The audit cannot tell those apart from genuinely supported claims; this is the structural limit of an entity-only proxy. Both residuals are consistent with the finding of Kang and Choi (2023) that LLM factual recall is tightly coupled with subject-object co-occurrence in pretraining text. A sentence whose entities frequently co-occur lies inside the model’s reliable recall regime. One whose entities never co-occur lies outside it. Eq. (2) reads off this regime difference at training time, and the monotone five-bucket calibration shows the read-off is well-aligned with the reward sign.

B.6 Qualitative Case Study

This subsection presents two complementary qualitative views of the co-occurrence reward. (a) Figure 7 shows three illustrative single-sentence cases from the zero-frequency bucket where the co-occurrence reward catches a factual error that an LLM-as-judge misses, evidence that the entity-only Infini-gram lookup can detect fabrications that even a GPT-4o-mini-class judge confidently affirms. (b) Cases 1–2 below then trace the per-sentence reward through two complete training-time completions, showing correctly-flagged fabrications and one example (Case 1, sentence 2) of the first-triplet vs. multi-triplet trade-off quantified in §6.4.

(a) Single-sentence comparison vs. LLM judge.

Figure 7 illustrates three sentences from the zero-frequency bucket where the co-occurrence reward correctly identifies a factual error that an LLM judge misses. In each case the model generates a sentence containing a plausible but incorrect entity: a wrong zip code, a wrong cast member, a misspelled surname. GPT-4o-mini, given only the sentence text with no gold answer or surrounding context, confidently affirms each sentence as factually correct. The Infini-gram co-occurrence lookup, by contrast, returns zero co-occurrence for the fabricated subject-object pair, assigning ric=−0.3r_{i}^{\mathrm{c}}=-0.3. These cases represent 25 out of 152 human-confirmed incorrect sentences in the zero-frequency bucket where the LLM judge fails to detect the error (Table 12). The three sentences are isolated single-sentence examples, not complete model completions; the full per-sentence trace on complete completions is given in part (b) below.

(b) Full per-sentence trace on two completions.

The two cases below trace the per-sentence reward through complete TriviaQA completions of Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct CorVer. Case 1 covers a fabricated proper name (sentence 3, ci=0c_{i}=0) correctly flagged with −0.3-0.3, plus a sentence (Case 1, sentence 2) whose extracted triplet is correct but whose surrounding details are wrong, illustrating the first-triplet vs. multi-triplet trade-off resolved in favor of First in §6.4. Case 2 is a clean positive trace ending in a correctly-flagged category-mismatch fabrication (sentence 4, ci=0c_{i}=0).

B.7 Optional LLM Judge

We use a separate LLM judge only as an offline validation tool, not in the training loop. The judge is GPT-4o-mini at temperature 00. For each sentence we present only the sentence text and ask the model to label it CORRECT or INCORRECT. The gold answer and the surrounding QA context are intentionally withheld. The judgment therefore reflects the model’s own factual reliance, comparable to the regime that motivates the co-occurrence reward (§B.5). Outputs are parsed by a strict CORRECT / INCORRECT case-insensitive match. The same GPT-4o-mini judge is used to produce the LLM-affirms-incorrect column reported in the single-sentence case study (Figure 7). The training judge remains a string-match grader for every Raw ++ RL run reported in the paper; LLM-as-judge is never inside the GRPO reward loop.

Appendix C Results, Diagnostics, and Cost

C.1 Checkpoint Selection

We use a fixed end-of-run selection criterion across all models, not a held-out validation sweep. For every CorVer run (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-8B, OLMo-2-13B-Instruct, Qwen3-14B) we evaluate only the step-100100 checkpoint. Intermediate step-5050 checkpoints are saved every 5050 steps but are not graded post hoc. The same final-checkpoint policy is applied uniformly: no per-model best-of-checkpoints sweep is performed and no held-out development split is used to pick checkpoints. To justify this choice empirically, we extend a single run (Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct CorVer) to 300300 GRPO steps and evaluate every 5050 steps on TriviaQA. Figure 8 and Table 14 report the resulting trajectory: the first 100100 steps account for the bulk of the gain over the raw model (+6.85+6.85 pp), step 200200 is the empirical peak (+8.46+8.46 pp, a further +1.61+1.61 pp over the step-100100 checkpoint), and steps 250250–300300 exhibit a mild downward drift. Step 100100 therefore captures most of the improvement at one third of the compute, while step 200200 is a reasonable choice when compute is not the binding constraint. We adopt step 100100 for all six canonical runs reported in the paper.

C.2 Full Per-Model Results

Table 15 reports the raw and CorVer-trained accuracies on the five closed-book QA datasets for each canonical model, along with the NA (refusal) rate at evaluation. The Raw column is the instruction-tuned base model under the eval prompt of §A.3 at temperature 0.00.0; the CorVer column is the step-100100 checkpoint of the canonical CorVer run for that model.

For a compact side-by-side view of the same accuracies (Raw vs CorVer, with the better of the two within each pair in bold), see Table 16. NA rates are omitted in that view; refer to Table 15 above for the per-cell refusal-rate diagnostics, including the Qwen3-8B Raw NA-rate pattern referenced in §5.2.

C.3 Refusal-Rate Decomposition on Qwen3-8B

Table 17 shows that Qwen3-8B Raw refuses a substantial fraction of questions (up to 28%28\% on SimpleQA), while CorVer reduces the refusal rate to below 5%5\% on every benchmark. To verify that this reduced abstention reflects genuine recall rather than indiscriminate guessing, we examine the subset of questions that Qwen3-8B Raw refused but CorVer attempted. On this subset, CorVer achieves 24.9%24.9\% accuracy on TriviaQA, 17.5%17.5\% on NQ-Open, and 7.0%7.0\% on PopQA. These rates are well above chance for open-domain QA, confirming that CorVer unlocks recall on questions the raw model declined to attempt. The Llama family exhibits the opposite NA-rate shift (a modest increase of 33 to 55 pp), so its accuracy gain derives primarily from improved recall on attempted questions rather than from changes in abstention behavior.

C.4 Reward Cost Measurement Protocol

Figure 4 of the main text compares CorVer’s average training time against four factuality-RL baselines across four base models. This appendix provides four supplementary breakdowns: a qualitative cost profile per method class, the full per-cell cross-method wall-clock table (Table 18), per-cell GPU configurations (Table 19), and CorVer’s internal cost decomposition across its ablation variants (Table 20).

Qualitative cost profile. CorVer performs one 0.50.5B extractor forward pass and one mmap CNF count per sentence. Both are millisecond-scale on a single A100 and require no GPU reward model in the GRPO loop. NLI- and LLM-judge-based rewards require a neural forward pass (or an external API call) per generated sentence. At G=16G=16 completions ×\times multiple sentences per completion, this dominates the reward-call budget. KnowRL-style knowledge-verification RL additionally couples retrieval, candidate scoring, and verification into the reward path. The CorVer design is therefore deliberately positioned to keep sentence-level reward cost at the same order of magnitude as a standard outcome-only GRPO reward, not at the order of magnitude of neural-verifier or LLM-judge rewards.

Full cross-method table. Table 18 reports the end-to-end training hours required to produce each method’s checkpoint in Table 1 across the four base models of Figure 4. Parenthetical values in baseline cells are CorVer’s speedup over that cell. The final column averages each baseline’s per-model speedup ratio.

GPU configuration. CorVer and KnowRL ran on a single A100 for every base model. FoRAG, RLFH, and FSPO ran on a single A100 in most configurations; three runs (FoRAG and RLFH on Qwen3-8B, FSPO on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) OOM’d and were moved to a single H200. Per-cell assignments are given in Table 19.

Internal cost decomposition. Table 20 measures the wall-clock cost of CorVer’s ablation variants on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct at 100100 GRPO steps. Removing the QuCo signal entirely (A1) cuts wall-clock roughly in half, so the per-sentence reward path dominates reward-side cost despite the cheap per-call rate. A3 averages the same per-sentence values into a response-level scalar but saves only about 30%30\% relative to the full method. The QuCo lookup is therefore incurred regardless of how its output reaches advantages, and per-token alignment adds only a small overhead on top. Combined with Table 2, this attributes the accuracy gain to alignment itself, not to the compute difference between alignment and averaging.

Appendix D Auxiliary Findings and Practical Lessons

Several engineering observations shaped the final CorVer recipe. We document them here for completeness; the mechanisms below are our interpretations from preliminary runs, not controlled experiments validating each claim.

(L1) Intermediate SFT cold-start hurt factual recall on knowledge QA in our setup.

We observed some unusual pattern for the wide-applicable SFT++GRPO pipeline (Hao et al., 2026). We collected chain-of-thought traces from a 397397B-parameter Qwen3-family MoE teacher and SFT-trained three smaller targets on these traces with LoRA, in two cases continuing with GRPO from the SFT checkpoint. Table 21 reports the resulting TriviaQA accuracies. The SFT-only checkpoint loses between 77 and 1818 pp relative to the raw instruction-tuned baseline on every target. The subsequent GRPO stage recovers part of the gap on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-4B but does not reach the raw baseline in either case. Our tentative interpretation is a capacity mismatch: the student lacks the teacher’s reasoning capacity but is forced to mimic complex reasoning chains it cannot execute reliably, so questions it would have answered without reasoning may be lost to forced-but-incorrect deliberation. We do not claim this generalizes. The same degradation could also reflect our specific SFT data composition (long deliberative traces vs. the short factual answers the target needs at inference), the SFT hyperparameters we used (epoch counts, LoRA rank, learning rate, none of which we swept), the specific teacher choice, or the inconsistent SFT starting point in our Qwen3 runs (the SFT-only Qwen3 rows use the −-Base variants while the SFT++GRPO Qwen3 rows use the −-Instruct variants; see Table 21 caption). We report Table 21 as an interesting empirical pattern that motivated the raw-model recipe used in the main results, not as a controlled finding that SFT cold-start is generally harmful for knowledge-intensive RL.

(L2) Anti-loop instructions had opposite effects on raw and CorVer-trained policies.

Adding an anti-loop instruction (“Do not loop or repeat the same point or phrase”) to the eval prompt had opposite effects on the two policy regimes in our runs. The raw (un-trained) instruction-tuned models did not exhibit looping behavior, and appending the line produced a small accuracy decrease on every target. We presume the extra rule simply adds prompt complexity that the un-trained policy is not robust to. CorVer-trained checkpoints, by contrast, occasionally fell into low-diversity repetition on long-form completions, and the same anti-loop line empirically blocked this without changing the policy weights. Our hypothesized mechanism is reward exploitation: the per-sentence co-occurrence reward (Eq. (2)) incentivizes well-supported sentences, and the trained policy may learn to repeat one such sentence to harvest the reward signal on every repeated token. We therefore use the lighter prompt for every raw baseline (its strongest configuration) and the anti-loop prompt for every trained checkpoint. This asymmetry makes the Raw vs CorVer gaps in Table 1 a conservative lower bound; see Appendix A.3 for the prompt diff.

(L3) Small models (3B/4B) needed fully-mastered anchor questions in our runs to avoid training collapse.

Training Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and Qwen3-4B on the learning-zone-only pool (the ncorrect∈[1,G−1]n_{\mathrm{correct}}\in[1,G-1] subset alone) led to training collapse in preliminary runs: accuracy degraded over training rather than improving. Mixing 1,0001{,}000 (800800 for Qwen3-4B) fully-mastered (ncorrect=Gn_{\mathrm{correct}}=G) anchor questions back into the training pool stabilized the run and produced the gains reported in Table 1. Anchor questions carry no within-group advantage signal under GRPO and are formally redundant. The empirical interpretation is that they act as a distributional anchor: they keep the small-model policy close to the raw-model response distribution while the learning-zone prompts drive correctness gains. Larger models (≥8\geq 8B) trained successfully on the learning-zone-only pool and did not require anchors. The exact per-model anchor counts are listed in Appendix A.4.
